flashcards.q: Why does Amazon's PR/FAQ format start with a press release before any implementation detail?
flashcards.a: Writing the announcement first forces the author to articulate the customer-facing value proposition in plain language before getting lost in implementation detail -- if the value proposition can't be stated clearly, that's an early, cheap signal the idea isn't ready, delivered in hours instead of months.

flashcards.q: Why does a written one-pager/memo, read silently before discussion, produce better decisions than a live slide presentation?
flashcards.a: It produces a more independent read from each attendee, not anchored by who spoke first or delivery confidence. It also forces the author to resolve ambiguity in full sentences that a bullet-point deck lets slide -- the document has to stand on its own.

flashcards.q: What four vocabulary terms does a business case need to speak finance's language, beyond engineering merit?
flashcards.a: Payback period (comparable across different proposal types), NPV (fair comparison across different time horizons/risk), a risk-adjusted RANGE with stated confidence and source (not a fake-precise point estimate), and explicit opportunity cost (what else the resource could do).

flashcards.q: Describe the four roles in a stakeholder map for moving a decision you don't own.
flashcards.a: Decider (whose actual 'yes' approves it, often ONE person), Approver/Blocker (can green-light or veto a specific piece -- security, legal, a dependent team), Allies (amplify with minimal convincing), Skeptics (need real evidence, objections worth surfacing early).

flashcards.q: What is the correct pre-wiring order before a group decision meeting, and why?
flashcards.a: Allies first (cheap, low-stakes feedback that sharpens the pitch), then Skeptics in 1:1s (their objection caught privately is a gift you can address before it costs credibility live), then Approvers/Blockers, then the Decider -- who should ideally hear the substance informally before the formal room.

flashcards.q: What makes a proposal an 'easy yes' for a hesitant Decider?
flashcards.a: Minimizing what the Decider personally risks: propose the smallest reversible version first (a time-boxed pilot, not a year-long commitment), include your own kill criteria/checkpoint, and name competing priorities explicitly with a sequencing argument rather than pretending nothing else is competing for the resource.

flashcards.q: What is the 'how did you get there' or tactical-rebuttal technique, and when is it more effective than arguing directly?
flashcards.a: Asking a decision-maker to walk through their reasoning surfaces information/constraints you may not have, rather than risking an argument against a strawman of their actual position. More effective when you suspect they have context you don't (budget, other stakeholders, political factors) -- common in real orgs.

flashcards.q: You've made your case, been heard, and been overruled. What's the senior move, and why does it matter beyond this one decision?
flashcards.a: State disagreement once, clearly, then execute the decision fully with no relitigating or passive undermining. Credibility for future influence is a finite, reputational resource -- someone known for accepting a loss badly gets less benefit of the doubt next time they push back, exactly when it might matter more.

flashcards.q: Why does a risk-adjusted range with stated confidence beat a confident point estimate in a business case?
flashcards.a: Finance reviewers are professionally trained to distrust suspiciously precise, unsourced numbers. A range with a named basis ('likely $200-400K, moderate confidence, based on X') survives scrutiny because you can defend where it came from; a fabricated point estimate collapses the first time someone asks its source.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT spend your influence capital trying to change a decision, even if you disagree?
flashcards.a: When the decision is small and easily reversible (low cost of being wrong), when your own confidence isn't actually high, or when you've recently spent significant capital elsewhere -- influence capital is finite and reputational, and indiscriminate spending depletes it for the decision that actually matters most.
